statement: pytest is a command-line test framework that automatically discovers the tests you have written, runs them, and reports the results.
In pytest you use a plain assert statement to make a test fail, rather than specialized methods such as self.assertEqual() or self.assertLessThan().
pytest can run tests that were written for the unittest or nose frameworks, so an existing test suite need not be rewritten to adopt pytest.
Install pytest with pip into the virtual environment you are using for testing (e.g. pip install pytest).
condition: you are working inside a project virtual environment

statement: Because pytest is installed separately from your Python interpreter, you can run the same latest pytest version against legacy Python 2 (2.6+) and Python 3 (3.3+).
Run pytest with -v (or --verbose) to get more detailed output, including the full diff of a failing assertion.
condition: you need more detail than the default one-character-per-test output

statement: On Windows, activate the virtual environment with venv\\Scripts\\activate.bat instead of the POSIX 'source venv/bin/activate'.
condition: you are on Windows

statement: From Python 3.6 onward the standard-library venv module can be used instead of installing virtualenv, though some platforms still behave better with virtualenv.
exception: some platforms still behave better with virtualenv

statement: pytest reports a failing test in its own FAILURES section, pinpointing the first failing assertion and marking exactly which values differ.
Direct most of your testing at the layer just below the user interface (the API / subcutaneous layer) rather than at the final end-user interface.
pytest can be used for all types and levels of testing: unit, integration, system/end-to-end, and functional testing.
Run with no arguments and pytest recursively searches the current directory and all subdirectories for test files.
Give pytest a filename, directory, or list of them and it searches there instead of the current directory, recursively traversing each named directory.
For test files to be discovered, name them test_<something>.py or <something>_test.py.
For test functions and methods to be discovered, name them test_<something>.
For test classes to be discovered, name them Test<Something>.
Run a single test by specifying the file followed by ::<test_name> (e.g. pytest tasks/test_four.py::test_asdict).
pytest test outcomes are PASSED (.), FAILED (F), SKIPPED (s), xfail (x), XPASS (X), and ERROR (E).
An ERROR outcome means an exception occurred outside the test function itself, in a fixture or a hook function.
Use -k EXPRESSION to run only tests whose names match a substring expression; the expression supports 'and', 'or', and 'not'.
Use -m MARKEXPR to run only tests matching a marker expression, which also supports 'and', 'or', and 'not' (e.g. -m 'mark1 and not mark2').
Mark a subset of tests with the @pytest.mark.<name> decorator so they can be selected and run together, even across separate files.
Use -x (--exitfirst) to stop the entire test session immediately on the first failing test or error.
condition: you want to stop on first failure, e.g. when debugging

statement: Use --maxfail=num to stop the session after a given number of failures or errors rather than after the first.
By default pytest captures test output and only displays it for failing tests; use -s (a shortcut for --capture=no) to let print/stdout output show while tests run.
Use -l (--showlocals) to display local variables and their values in the tracebacks of failing tests.
Use --lf (--last-failed) to rerun only the tests that failed on the previous run.
Use --ff (--failed-first) to run the previously failed tests first and then the rest of the tests.
Use -v (--verbose) to get one line per test with the full test name and outcome instead of a single character.
Use -q (--quiet) to decrease reported output; it pairs well with --tb=line, which reports just the failing line.
Use --tb=style to control traceback format; the styles auto, long, short, line, native, and no are available, with auto being the default.
--tb=no removes tracebacks entirely and --tb=line reduces each failure to one line, which helps reveal patterns when many tests fail.
condition: you have many failing tests and want a compact view

statement: Use --durations=N to report the N slowest tests, setups, and teardowns after a run (--durations=0 reports all), which helps when speeding up a suite.
condition: you are trying to speed up the test suite

statement: Every pytest test has three phases: setup, call, and teardown, where setup and teardown are provided by fixtures.
Use --collect-only to show which tests would run under the current options without executing them, e.g. to verify that a -k selection is correct.
condition: you want to confirm a test-selection option before running

statement: Use pytest --markers to list available markers and pytest --fixtures to list available fixtures.
pytest -h (--help) shows usage plus command-line options, ini-file options, and environment variables, and it expands to include options added by installed plugins.
The options, markers, and fixtures available can change depending on the target directory or file, because pytest loads conftest.py files found along that path.
conftest.py and ini files (such as pytest.ini) let you customize pytest behavior locally to a project or even to a subset of its tests.
Keep test files in a directory separate from the package source (e.g. tests/ vs src/); this is a best practice rather than a pytest requirement.
exception: pytest does not require this separation

statement: Separate functional and unit tests into their own directories so a subset can be run easily; functional tests should break only when functionality is intentionally changed, whereas unit tests may break during refactoring.
exception: the directory split is arbitrary and not required

statement: A setup.py file is required to install a package locally so that it (and its modules) become importable by the test code.
Install the package under test locally with pip (pip install . or from one directory up pip install ./project/) so tests can import it.
Install the package in editable mode (pip install -e .) when you want to modify its source while it stays installed.
condition: you want to keep editing the package source while it is installed

statement: pytest.ini is optional, holds project-wide pytest configuration, and there should be at most one per project.
conftest.py is optional and is treated by pytest as a local plugin that can contain hook functions and fixtures.
Hooks and fixtures shared by tests across multiple subdirectories should live in tests/conftest.py, and you may have multiple conftest.py files (one per subdirectory).
In test functions use a plain 'assert <expression>' as the primary way to signal failure; the test fails if the expression evaluates falsy.
pytest's assert rewriting intercepts assert calls and reports detailed information about why an assertion failed, including the exact failing line and a value diff.
Assert on the failing test with -v to get the full diff when the default output truncates the compared values.
condition: the default failure output omits part of the diff

statement: Assert that a block raises an expected exception with 'with pytest.raises(<ExpectedException>):'; the test fails if no exception or a different exception is raised.
Capture the raised exception with 'as excinfo' (an ExceptionInfo object) to inspect it, e.g. checking excinfo.value.args[0] against the expected message.
A test function may carry multiple markers, and the same marker may be applied to many test functions.
Apply a custom marker with the @pytest.mark.<name> decorator, then select those tests with -m <name>.
A smoke test is, by convention, a quick non-exhaustive subset of tests that gives a fast read on the overall health of the system.
Tests marked with the same marker in different files can all be selected and run together with -m.
pytest provides the builtin markers skip, skipif, and xfail.
Apply @pytest.mark.skip(reason=...) to unconditionally skip a test so it is not even attempted.
Apply @pytest.mark.skipif(<expression>, reason=...) to skip a test when a Python expression is true; the reason argument is required for skipif (optional for skip).
condition: the skip should be conditional on a runtime expression

statement: Include a reason for every skip, skipif, and xfail marker.
Apply @pytest.mark.xfail(...) to run a test but declare it expected to fail; it reports as xfail (x) when it fails and XPASS (X) when it unexpectedly passes.
Set xfail_strict=true in pytest.ini so that a test marked xfail which actually passes is reported as a FAIL.
condition: you want unexpected passes of xfail tests treated as failures

statement: Use -rs (a form of -r chars) to show the short summary with the reasons for skipped tests and other selected outcomes.
You can run a subset of tests by selecting a directory, file, class, individual test, or a name expression, in addition to markers.
Run all tests in a directory by passing that directory path as an argument to pytest.
Run pytest with -v to see the exact node-id syntax for invoking a specific directory, class, or test.
A fixture declared with autouse=True is applied to all tests within its scope without being requested by name.
In a fixture, code before the yield runs as setup before each test and code after the yield runs as teardown afterward; the yield can also pass data to the test.
pytest also supports old-style xUnit setup/teardown functions (as used by unittest and nose), but fixtures are the preferred pytest mechanism.
Group related tests in a test class, then run just that class with the node id file::ClassName.
Run a single method of a test class with the node id file::ClassName::method_name.
Use @pytest.mark.parametrize(argnames, argvalues) to run one test function against multiple data sets, with each set reported as a separate test.
The first argument to parametrize is a comma-separated string of parameter names and the second is the list of value sets to feed the test.
When parameter values convert cleanly to strings, pytest builds a readable test identifier from them; otherwise it falls back to indexed ids like task0, task1.
A parametrized test's full identifier (a node id) can be used to re-run just that one case; quote the identifier if it contains spaces, brackets, or parentheses.
condition: the identifier contains characters the shell would interpret

statement: Pass the ids parameter to parametrize (a list of strings the same length as the data sets) to supply your own readable case identifiers.
condition: the default identifier is not readable / cannot be derived from the value

statement: Use pytest.param(<value>, id="...") to attach a custom id alongside an individual parameter value.
parametrize can be applied to a test class so the same data sets are sent to all of its test methods.
Declare a fixture by decorating a function with @pytest.fixture(); a test requests it by listing the fixture name as a parameter, and pytest runs the fixture before the test.
A fixture can perform work and can return data to the test function that requests it.
Fixture naming is significant: pytest resolves a requested fixture by name first in the test's own module, then in conftest.py files.
A pytest test fixture is the mechanism for separating 'get ready for' and 'clean up after' code from the test functions themselves.
Put a fixture in a conftest.py file to share it across multiple test files; put it in a single test file to restrict it to that file.
Fixtures defined in a lower-level conftest.py are available to tests in that directory and its subdirectories.
Do not import conftest.py from test files; pytest reads it automatically as a local plugin.
In a yield-style fixture, the teardown code after the yield is guaranteed to run regardless of what happens during the tests.
Use the --setup-show flag to trace which fixtures run and in what setup and teardown order.
condition: you are developing or debugging fixtures

statement: In --setup-show output, F marks a function-scoped fixture and S marks a session-scoped fixture.
When a test fails, pytest reports the values of the function's parameters, which includes the fixtures it requested.
If an assert or other exception occurs inside a fixture, the test is reported as ERROR rather than FAIL, so a FAIL always means the failure was in the test body itself, not a fixture it depends on.
Structure the body of a test in a GIVEN/WHEN/THEN comment format when the intent is not obvious from the code alone.
Use the builtin tmpdir fixture to obtain a temporary directory that pytest cleans up automatically, avoiding manual teardown.
tmpdir yields a directory object (not a string) that implements __str__, so wrap it in str() when a plain path string is needed.
Fixtures can be consumed directly by tests or requested by other fixtures, allowing fixtures to build on one another.
Push as much test setup (the GIVEN) into fixtures as possible so that a test can only FAIL because the behaviour under test broke, not because setup failed (which reports as ERROR).
The scope parameter to @pytest.fixture() controls how often a fixture is set up and torn down; its values are function, class, module, and session, with function being the default.
A function-scoped fixture runs once per test function; a class-scoped fixture runs once per test class; a module-scoped fixture runs once per module; a session-scoped fixture runs once per session.
A fixture's scope is fixed at its definition, not at the place where it is used; the tests that request a fixture cannot control how often it is set up and torn down.
A fixture may only depend on other fixtures of the same or a wider scope (e.g. a function-scoped fixture can use a session-scoped one, but not the reverse).
exception: you cannot make a wider-scoped fixture depend on a narrower-scoped one

statement: Do expensive setup once in a session-scoped fixture and pair it with a small function-scoped fixture that resets state (e.g. delete all rows) before each test, to avoid rebuilding costly resources per test.
condition: the expensive resource can be safely reset between tests

statement: Use the session-scoped tmpdir_factory (rather than the function-scoped tmpdir) when you need a temporary directory at session scope.
condition: you need a temporary directory shared across the session

statement: Mark a test or class with @pytest.mark.usefixtures('f1','f2') to activate fixtures without listing them in the parameter list.
A fixture activated via usefixtures cannot supply its return value to the test; only fixtures listed in the parameter list can provide their return value.
exception: fixtures requested through usefixtures give no access to their return value

statement: Set autouse=True to make a fixture run for every test in its scope without being named, which suits code that must run at certain times but whose data the tests do not depend on.
condition: tests do not need the fixture's return value or explicit dependency

statement: Prefer named (explicitly requested) fixtures and treat autouse as the exception rather than the rule.
Rename a fixture with the name parameter to @pytest.fixture(name='...') so tests can reference a shorter or clearer name than the function name.
Use the --fixtures option (optionally with a test filename) to list all fixtures available to a test and where each is defined.
condition: you need to discover or locate available fixtures

statement: Parametrize a fixture with @pytest.fixture(params=[...]); every test that uses the fixture then runs once per parameter value, which the fixture reads from request.param.
request is a builtin fixture representing the calling state of a fixture; its param field holds the current value when the fixture is parametrized.
Supply the ids parameter to a parametrized fixture (a list of strings, or a function invoked per value) to generate readable identifiers for each parametrized run.
Parametrizing a fixture multiplies every test that uses it, whereas parametrizing a test multiplies only that single test.
Isolate an environment or backend choice inside a single fixture and parametrize that fixture (e.g. params=['tiny','mongo']) to run the entire suite against each option.
With -v, pytest labels each parametrized run by its parametrization value, which reads cleanly when the values are strings.

pytest ships builtin fixtures for common needs such as temporary files, accessing command-line options, communicating between test sessions, validating output streams, modifying environment variables, and interrogating warnings.
Reusing common fixtures is valuable enough that pytest bundles frequently needed fixtures as builtins.
The tmpdir builtin fixture returns a py.path.local object giving a temporary directory unique to each test-function invocation.
Because tmpdir is function-scoped, it cannot create files or directories that must outlive a single test; use tmpdir_factory for class, module, or session scope.
condition: the temporary files must persist beyond one test function

statement: Create a temporary directory in a wider scope with tmpdir_factory.mktemp('name'), which returns a py.path.local like tmpdir; tmpdir_factory.getbasetemp() returns the session base directory.
pytest retains only the most recent few temporary base directories and cleans up older ones, so you can still inspect files after a recent run.
Override the temporary base directory with pytest --basetemp=mydir.
condition: you need control over where temp files are created

statement: To get a module- or class-scoped temporary directory, write your own fixture of that scope that itself uses tmpdir_factory.
When a single temporary data file serves multiple tests, build it once in a wider-scope fixture rather than recreating it for each test.
The pytestconfig builtin fixture (a shortcut to request.config) gives access to command-line arguments and options, configuration files, plugins, and the launch directory.
Add a custom command-line option with the pytest_addoption hook (parser.addoption(...)) and read its value in a test via pytestconfig.getoption('name').
Add command-line options via pytest_addoption only in a plugin or in the top-level conftest.py, never in a test subdirectory.
exception: do not add options from a conftest.py in a test subdirectory

statement: Because pytestconfig is a fixture, it can be requested from other fixtures, letting you wrap option values in named fixtures.
Keep tests independent and order-independent so any test can be run or rerun in any order and produce the same result, and sessions stay repeatable.
Use the cache builtin fixture to deliberately pass information from one test session to the next; the --lf and --ff options are built on this mechanism.
condition: you intentionally want cross-session state

statement: The cache fixture interface is cache.get(key, default) and cache.set(key, value).
By convention a cache key begins with your application or plugin name and separates sections with '/', and stored values must be JSON-serializable.
Use --cache-show to display cache contents and --cache-clear to remove all cache contents at the start of a run.
request.node.nodeid is a unique test identifier that works even for parametrized tests; sanitize characters such as colons before using it in a cache key or filename.
The cache fixture is function-scoped, but request.config.cache is the same underlying object and can be used from a fixture of any scope.
Use the capsys builtin fixture to capture and assert on stdout and stderr from code under test, retrieving them with out, err = capsys.readouterr().
capsys.readouterr() returns the output captured since the start of the function or since the last time it was called.
Use capsys.disabled() as a context manager to let specific output bypass pytest's capture mechanism.
condition: you need certain output printed even while capture is on

statement: Use the monkeypatch builtin fixture to modify environment variables, attributes, or dictionary items for the duration of a test, with the changes automatically undone afterward.
monkeypatch.setenv(name, value) sets an environment variable for the test only.
monkeypatch.setattr(obj, name, value) replaces an attribute during the test (e.g. patching os.path.expanduser with a lambda).
monkeypatch.setitem(dict, key, value) changes a dictionary item just for the duration of the test.
monkeypatch provides matching del forms (delenv, delattr, delitem) that remove an environment variable, attribute, or dictionary item instead of setting one.
monkeypatch.syspath_prepend(path) prepends a path to sys.path so code under test imports a stub version of a module first.
condition: you want to shadow a real module with a stub

statement: monkeypatch.chdir(path) changes the current working directory during the test, which helps when testing scripts that depend on the cwd.
condition: the code under test depends on the current working directory

statement: The raising parameter on monkeypatch methods controls whether an exception is raised when the targeted item does not already exist.
Do not run a side-effecting function against the real environment (e.g. writing to the user's real home-directory file); redirect it to a temporary location so the test cannot clobber real user data.

Prefer patching the specific function a module calls (e.g. expanduser) over patching a broad, OS-dependent environment variable (e.g. HOME) when the environment approach behaves differently across platforms.
condition: the environment-variable approach is operating-system dependent

statement: You can combine monkeypatch with unittest.mock to temporarily replace attributes with mock objects.
doctest lets you embed runnable code examples in docstrings; run them under pytest with the --doctest-modules flag.
pytest treats each docstring that contains code as a separate doctest test.
Use the doctest_namespace builtin fixture inside an autouse fixture in a top-level conftest.py to inject symbols (such as import aliases) into the doctest namespace without cluttering the docstrings.
condition: doctests rely on names not imported within each docstring

statement: Use the recwarn builtin fixture to examine warnings issued by code under test; it behaves like a list of warnings, each exposing category, message, filename, and lineno.
recwarn collects warnings from the start of the test; call recwarn.clear() to reset the list before the section where you actually want to capture warnings.
condition: the relevant warnings occur later in the test

statement: Alternatively, use the pytest.warns() context manager to assert that a specific block of code issues a warning; recwarn and pytest.warns() are equivalent, so the choice is a matter of taste.
Any fixtures or hook functions placed in a project's top-level conftest.py already form a local conftest plugin; converting that file into an installable package lets you share it across projects.
Find third-party pytest plugins on PyPI (search 'pytest-' or '-pytest'), on the pytest documentation plugins page, and in the pytest-dev group on GitHub.
Install pytest plugins with pip like any other package, pinning a specific version with ==<version> when needed.
Install a plugin offline from a local directory of .tar.gz/.whl files with pip install --no-index --find-links=./dir <plugin>, which suits CI, tox, or your own custom plugins.
condition: you cannot or do not want to fetch from PyPI

statement: Install a plugin directly from a Git repository (pip install git+https://.../repo, optionally @tag or @branch) when it is not on PyPI or you keep your own plugin in Git.
condition: the plugin or version is not published on PyPI

statement: pytest plugins alter behavior through hook functions, and pytest exposes many hooks documented on the pytest site.
Prototype a behavior change in conftest.py first, then move the working code into a package to turn it into a distributable plugin.
A minimal installable pytest plugin needs a module file (e.g. pytest_nice.py) and a setup.py.
Register a plugin with pytest through the setuptools entry_points 'pytest11' group (e.g. entry_points={'pytest11': ['nice = pytest_nice']}); pytest11 is the special identifier pytest looks for.
Implement plugin behavior with pytest hook functions such as pytest_addoption, pytest_report_header, and pytest_report_teststatus.
A pytest plugin's setup.py needs the version, url, license, py_modules (or packages), and one of the author/author_email or maintainer/maintainer_email pairs.
Use py_modules for a single-module plugin and switch to packages (a directory of modules) when the plugin has more than one module.
condition: the plugin comprises more than one module

statement: setuptools requires some form of README file (README, README.rst, or README.txt) or it emits a warning when building a distribution.
Plugins are code and must be tested like any other code.
Enable pytest's bundled pytester plugin (disabled by default) by adding pytest_plugins = 'pytester' to the test suite's conftest.py.
condition: you are writing automated tests for a plugin

statement: With pytester enabled, use the testdir fixture (which creates a temporary directory) and testdir.makepyfile("""...""") to write an example test file.
Run pytest programmatically against the generated example with testdir.runpytest(options), which returns a RunResult object.
Assert on a plugin run's output with result.stdout.fnmatch_lines([...]) (glob wildcards allowed) and check result.ret, where 0 means all tests passed and 1 means some failed.
The general pattern for testing a plugin is: create an example test file, run pytest against it with or without options, examine the output, and check the exit code.
Keep each test checking a single thing, giving distinct concerns their own separate test functions.
Install a plugin (pip install . or in editable mode) before running its test suite.
Build a source distribution of a plugin with 'python setup.py sdist', which produces a .tar.gz in the dist/ directory.
Upgrade a plugin installed from a shared directory by adding --upgrade to pip install --no-index --find-links <dir> <plugin>.
condition: a newer version exists in the shared directory

statement: Scaffold a distributable pytest plugin with cookiecutter-pytest-plugin, which is maintained by the pytest core team.
condition: you are creating a plugin to distribute widely

statement: Place an __init__.py in every test subdirectory to allow identical test filenames to exist in multiple test directories without collision.
You can store pytest configuration in tox.ini instead of a separate pytest.ini, saving one configuration file.
condition: you use tox

statement: You can store pytest configuration in setup.cfg (ini format), which is convenient when a project already has one for distribution.
condition: you already distribute the package with a setup.cfg

statement: The pytest configuration format is largely the same regardless of whether it lives in pytest.ini, tox.ini, or setup.cfg.
Override test-file discovery with the python_files ini setting (default: files starting test_ or ending _test), e.g. python_files = test_* *_test check_*.
Override test-class discovery with the python_classes ini setting (default Test*), e.g. python_classes = *Test Test* *Suite.
Override test-function and method discovery with the python_functions ini setting (default test_*), e.g. adding check_*.
Change pytest's default naming conventions only for a strong reason such as migrating hundreds of existing test files; otherwise leave the defaults.
exception: a large existing suite with a different convention justifies changing them

statement: Migrate a naming convention gradually by listing both the old and new patterns in the discovery ini setting.
condition: you are transitioning an existing suite to a new naming scheme

statement: Set xfail_strict = true and treat it as something to always enable, so an xfail-marked test that passes is reported as an error.
Without __init__.py files, running pytest across multiple directories that share a test filename fails collection with an 'import file mismatch' error; adding empty __init__.py files fixes it.
Add __init__.py to test subdirectories as a habit rather than waiting until a duplicate-filename collision occurs.
Use the --pdb option to have pytest drop into an interactive pdb debugging session at the exact point of failure.
Speed up debugging failures by combining pytest options: --tb=style for traceback format, -v, -l for locals, --lf for last-failed, -x to stop first, and --pdb.
condition: you are diagnosing test failures

statement: Combine --lf -x --pdb to jump straight to the first previously failed test and debug it; without -x, pytest reopens pdb at each subsequent failure.
At the (Pdb) prompt, useful commands include p/pp (print/pretty-print), l/list, a/args, u/up, d/down, and q/quit; step and next add little value when stopped at an assert.
Code coverage measures the percentage of the code under test that the suite exercises and reveals which parts are completely untested.
coverage.py is the preferred Python coverage tool; drive it from pytest via the pytest-cov plugin.
Installing pytest-cov also installs coverage.py, since coverage is one of its dependencies.
Run pytest --cov=<source-dir> to produce a coverage report scoped to just that source directory.
Generate a browsable HTML coverage report with --cov-report=html (written to htmlcov/) to see exactly which lines are missed.
condition: you need line-level detail on what is untested

statement: Striving for 100% code coverage can be dangerous: untested code may signal either a missing test or unneeded functionality, and coverage analysis does not replace thinking.
Use mocks (test doubles such as spies, fakes, and stubs) to swap out parts of the system and isolate the code under test.
Between pytest's monkeypatch fixture and the mock package you have all the test-double functionality you typically need.
The mock package is in the standard library as unittest.mock from Python 3.3 onward; earlier versions use the PyPI 'mock' backport for the same functionality.
For pytest specifically, the pytest-mock plugin offers conveniences that make it a preferred interface to the mock system.
Tests that use mocks are necessarily white-box tests, because you must look into the code to decide what to mock and where.
Decide a testing strategy up front (for example, do most functionality testing at the API layer and mock that layer when testing the CLI) rather than fully retesting every layer.
Use the addopts setting in the [pytest] config section to always apply a chosen set of command-line options (e.g. -rsxX -l --tb=short --strict).
Use the --strict option to require that every marker used in tests be declared first, which catches marker typos.
Declare markers in the markers section of the pytest configuration file.
Install tox with pip (it can live in a virtual environment) and run the whole environment matrix by simply running tox.

tox builds a source distribution, creates a separate virtualenv per target environment (e.g. py27, py36), installs the package and its dependencies, runs the tests in each, and prints a per-environment pass/fail summary.
Adopt tox when testing packages that are intended to run in multiple environments.
condition: the package must work across multiple Python or dependency environments

statement: Continuous integration systems such as Jenkins are used to launch test suites after each code commit.
Produce the junit.xml results file that Jenkins and other CI systems need with pytest --junit-xml=<path>; that flag is the only thing required to generate it.
Use --junit-prefix to prepend a prefix to every test's classname in the junit-xml output, which helps separate results from different tox environments.
condition: you run the same tests across multiple environments

statement: Set junit_suite_name in the [pytest] config section to change the suite name that appears in junit-xml results (default 'pytest').
Keep CI build logic in a script under revision control rather than pasted directly into the CI job's execute block.
In CI, run pytest inside a virtual environment and install the project (e.g. pip install -e) before running the tests.
Test multiple environments from Jenkins either by setting up a separate job per environment or by having Jenkins call tox directly.
condition: you need to test more than one environment in CI

statement: pytest works as a unittest runner and can run both pytest-style and unittest-style tests in the same session.
Running unittest tests under pytest enables incremental migration: keep existing unittest tests, write new tests in pytest, and convert older ones gradually.

When mixing pytest fixtures and unittest in one session, session-scoped resources can conflict: a unittest tearDownModule and a pytest session-scope fixture may both try to tear down the same resource, causing an error depending on run order.
condition: pytest and unittest tests share a session-scoped resource

statement: Share a pytest session-scope fixture with a unittest.TestCase by adding a @pytest.mark.usefixtures('fixture') decorator at the class or method level.
Sharing a pytest fixture with unittest via usefixtures is only necessary for session-scope resources shared between unittest and pytest.
exception: not needed for resources not shared across the two frameworks

Automated deployment commonly includes provisioning, installing system dependencies, transferring artifacts, setting configuration and secrets, attaching storage, configuring networking, running migrations, and switching application versions.
Artifact transfer should be automated whether the artifact is source code, a built package, or a container image.
Environment variable placement is a deployment design decision that depends on whether the value belongs on the local machine, image, automation, or server.

Network configuration for a web app includes DNS and container/server port mapping.
Replacing the running application version should be an explicit deployment step, even if the simple approach is recreating a container.
More advanced deployments may require zero-downtime techniques, but the book’s simple workflow stops the old container and starts a new one.

statement: Pytest lets you write tests as simple functions without classes or inheritance, which is a major advantage over unittest for people getting started.

statement: Choose pytest over unittest because it supports plain test functions (no class inheritance required), has an extensible plugin ecosystem and reporting, and ships a fully-featured test runner, none of which unittest offers.

Pursuing 100% test coverage or strict full TDD is usually not worth the return on investment and may be unrealistic; experienced engineers are pragmatic and strike a balance where some testing is proper and no testing is foolish.
Complexity, purity and extremism (technical zealotry) tend to make a practice unsustainable; simpler heuristics work better because they can be sustained day after day.
Use object-oriented programming and class-based tests only where the paradigm fits (for example GUI applications); for many unit tests a functional approach with plain functions is simpler.
In xunit-style pytest tests, setup_function and teardown_function receive the test function as an argument and run before and after each test, letting you initialise and then delete per-test state.
Reset or delete per-test state in teardown so that a mutated test variable cannot cause a later test to pass or fail for the wrong reason.
Setup and teardown remove boilerplate from tests, and temporary print statements inside them are a simple way to observe and debug test execution.
Testing is a prerequisite for automation: reliable automated deployment depends on tests, and the build server is the intersection of testing and automation.
Run source-code quality reports and tests every time code is checked into source control, because check-in is the natural point to evaluate quality.
Use pytest verbosity flags (-v, -vv) selectively: prefer verbose output on the build server or when drilling into a specific failure, and default to normal verbosity locally to avoid distraction.

Measure coverage by installing pytest-cov and running it as a plugin (for example 'python -m pytest --cov=<pkg> tests/*.py'); the coverage report is a signal for deciding where tests are missing, not a mandate for 100%.
Include a linter (such as flake8 or pylint) in the testing process; a linter is a must-have that recovers some of the static checking an interpreted language like Python otherwise lacks.
flake8 by default reports both code-formatting issues and syntax bugs when pointed at source files.
When adopting pylint on an existing project, disable the refactor and convention categories (--disable=R,C) initially to focus on warnings and errors that indicate code which cannot execute.
condition: when first introducing pylint to a project

statement: A build should fail on code that cannot possibly execute; checking in non-executable code is never acceptable, and linters catch this.
Adopt an opinionated auto-formatter such as black to eliminate style debates: running it reformats code to a consistent standard and silences the linter's formatting complaints.
For quick, exploratory debugging a print statement (for example printing inputs with f-strings) is often the fastest and best way to inspect values.
condition: when toying with sample code or the bug is simple

statement: When print statements are not enough, insert the Python debugger with 'import pdb; pdb.set_trace()' to step through code line by line and inspect variables.
condition: when a print statement does not reveal the problem

statement: Run pytest with the --pdb flag to drop into the debugger at the point of a test failure, using the same pdb commands as a standalone session.

Pytest fixtures are helpers that supply data or behaviour to tests and are injected by declaring the fixture's name as a test-function argument; the argument name must match the fixture name exactly or injection fails.
Define a fixture by decorating a function with @pytest.fixture; the framework detects it at collection time and injects it into any test that names it.
Unit tests should be as contained and reproducible as possible, so reduce or eliminate dependencies on external services by substituting fakes or fixtures rather than making real requests.
Have a fixture return an inner factory function (a closure) so that tests can pass arguments to construct the object at test time instead of building it eagerly when the fixture is defined.
condition: when tests need to vary the constructed object's parameters

statement: When extending a fixture or fake to accept new parameters, give the new parameters sensible defaults so existing tests are not disrupted.
Start pytest plugins as simple functions and only promote them to a separate installable package once the functionality grows or more than one project can reuse it.
condition: when plugin functionality grows beyond a few functions or is reused across projects

statement: Pytest ships built-in fixtures (including monkeypatch, capsys and tmpdir/tmp_path) that any test can use by naming them; 'pytest -q --fixtures' lists what is available.
Extract shared per-test setup (such as initialising a git repository) into a fixture rather than copying a setup_class method across classes, to avoid duplicated code and improve reuse.

Give a fixture cleanup by declaring 'request' as an argument and registering a finalizer with request.addfinalizer(callable), wrapping the callable in a lambda so teardown runs after the test rather than immediately.
Prefer the built-in tmpdir/tmp_path fixture over manually creating temp directories, because it provides its own cleanup and avoids writing a potentially dangerous 'rm -rf' finalizer.

Set a fixture's scope to control how often it runs: 'function' once per test, 'class' once per class, 'module' once per module, and 'session' once per session; widen the scope for expensive setup that need not repeat per test.

When many tests make the same assertion with only the inputs changing, replace them with a single parametrized test using @pytest.mark.parametrize, which runs each input as its own independent test case.
condition: when tests repeat the same assertion across differing inputs

statement: Avoid using a for loop to make assertions across inputs, because a loop obscures which assertion is being made and stops at the first failure; parametrization reports each input separately and continues after failures.
Patching (monkeypatching) is needed when a dependency with the desired behaviour cannot be passed into the code as an argument.
If code is hard to test or requires heavy patching, treat it as a red flag that the code is insufficiently modular or has too many uncontrolled dependencies.
Treat testing as a first-class concern while writing new code, because considering testability during implementation makes the resulting function far easier to test.

Patch a name where it is used, not where it is defined: to replace something in my_project.utils you patch 'my_project.utils.<name>', reflecting how that module imported it, not the origin module path.

Use monkeypatch.setattr (by string path 'module.name' or by passing the imported module object and attribute name) to replace a callable at runtime; pytest restores the original after each test regardless of outcome.

To patch a dependency for every test automatically, define a fixture with @pytest.fixture(autouse=True) that uses monkeypatch and place it in conftest.py, so no per-test flag or configuration is needed.
condition: when a dependency must be stubbed globally across the whole test session

statement: monkeypatch provides safe, self-cleaning helpers beyond setattr, including delattr, setitem/delitem for dictionaries, setenv/delenv for environment variables, syspath_prepend and chdir, each restoring state after the test.
If a test needs more than about three patches, treat it as a signal to rethink the approach and refactor, because heavily-patched tests are brittle, hard to read, and defeat the purpose of testing.
condition: when a single test requires more than roughly three patches

statement: Prefer dependency injection over patching: allow dependencies to be passed as arguments with a default that falls back to the real one (for example 'def main(argv=None): argv = argv or sys.argv'), so tests inject fakes without any patching.

Do not patch built-in modules such as os, because doing so can alter behaviour in other libraries and the test framework itself; instead inject the dependency or extract the built-in call into a small wrapper.
For large, hard-to-test code, extract the specific functionality you need to exercise into a smaller testable unit rather than patching everything around a huge function.
Use tox to run a project's test suite across multiple Python versions, configured through an INI-style tox.ini whose [tox] envlist names the environments (for example py27, py35, py36).
Define a [testenv] section in tox.ini with 'deps' (test dependencies to install) and 'commands' (how to run the tests); these steps are repeated for every environment in envlist.

Test across multiple Python versions even within Python 3, because subtle behavioural differences (for example dict insertion-order guarantees changing between 3.5 and 3.6+) can surface bugs you would otherwise miss.
Dictionary insertion order was not guaranteed in early Python 3 versions and only became a guaranteed language feature from Python 3.7, so code must not assume ordered dicts on older interpreters.
condition: on Python versions before 3.7

statement: Build a multidimensional tox matrix compactly using factors: curly brackets expand combinations and dashes separate factors, so 'py{27,35,36,37,38}-release_{1.1,2.x}' generates every version-by-branch combination automatically.
Be careful that dashes separate tox factors: writing 'py38-release-2.0' creates three factors (py38, release, 2.0) instead of the intended two, causing configuration confusion.
Constrain envlist explicitly (for example 'py27-release_1.1, py{35,36,37,38}-release_2.x') to test only the intended version-branch pairs rather than the full cartesian product.

Use tox factor-specific dependencies to pin different tool versions per environment (for example 'py27: pytest<4.7' alongside 'py35,py36,py37,py38: pytest==5.3.4'), because a dependency may have dropped support for an older Python.
condition: when a dependency has stopped supporting an older Python version being tested

statement: Alternatively override a single environment with its own '[testenv:<name>]' section while the base [testenv] holds the defaults, to give one environment different dependencies or commands.
Add non-testing environments to tox (for example a 'flake8' linting environment and a 'docs' Sphinx-build environment) so tox orchestrates linting, docs and other validations, not just unit tests.
When building docs in CI, pass sphinx-build the -W flag to treat warnings as errors so the build returns a non-zero exit status on any warning.
condition: for documentation builds in continuous integration

statement: Continuous Integration is the automated building and testing of software on every change; Continuous Delivery extends it to also deploy the software to a new environment.
Drive both local and build-server workflows through the same commands (for example a Makefile with 'make lint' and 'make test'), because divergent local and remote setups add needless complexity.
Run tests, linting and formatting locally and ensure they pass before pushing to source control, so the build server confirms rather than first discovers quality problems.

Represent infrastructure as code (IaC, e.g. Terraform, Pulumi, CloudFormation) checked in alongside source, enabling fully automated environment provisioning and deployment with humans out of the loop.
All modern software systems should treat automated testing and Continuous Delivery as a requirement, as there are few if any valid reasons not to automate testing and deployment.
Write down and perform a deployment workflow manually first, then automate it, because you must understand the concrete steps before encoding them in a pipeline.
Do not check generated build artifacts into source control (for example a static-site 'public' directory); add them to .gitignore and provide a 'make clean' target to remove them.
After downloading a tool binary, run its version flag as a basic sanity check before relying on it.
Configure a source-control webhook so that pushes trigger the build, which is what makes delivery continuous (for example AWS CodeBuild deploying on every push).
Store the build/deploy definition as a checked-in configuration file (for example cloudbuild.yaml or buildspec.yml) alongside the source, so the pipeline is versioned with the code.

Pin tool versions in the pipeline (for example an explicit HUGO_VERSION in buildspec) rather than always pulling latest, to keep builds reproducible; verify the exact release rather than blindly copying commands.
Prefer an explicit deploy command that syncs and prunes stale files (for example 'aws s3 sync public/ s3://bucket --delete') so the deployed target matches the freshly built output.
condition: when a higher-level deploy command is unavailable or unreliable

statement: Test a Click command-line tool with click.testing.CliRunner: invoke the command with arguments and assert on both the exit_code (0 for success) and the captured output.
When testing a CLI, assert the process exit status separately from the command's textual output, because they verify different contracts.
A health check or functional test that exercises a real workflow can surface unexpected pathological behaviour (for example a home-grown ORM emitting exponentially growing SQL) that unit tests miss.
Never silently swallow all exceptions and exit with status 0; hiding errors this way is a severe anti-pattern that makes failures undebuggable — log errors instead.
When confronting a legacy mess, start by making the code lintable (for example 'pylint --disable=R,C'), because establishing a baseline of static checks is a necessary first step before deeper fixes.
Refactor tangled legacy code by extracting nested logic into functions, writing tests for them, and adding logging, because tests and logging build the infrastructure that reveals hidden bugs.
Use the debugger (import pdb; pdb.set_trace()) as the tool of last resort when neither tests nor logging reveal the cause of a failure.
condition: when tests and logging fail to reveal the issue

statement: Automatically run linting and testing on every check-in, and add logging, as baseline hygiene that prevents whole classes of production failures.
Avoid technical zealotry: there is no perfect methodology, what works in one situation may fail in another, so debug empirically and take nothing for granted.
Without tests you cannot know your software works; software assembled by repeatedly guessing until it appears to run may still harbour subtle logic or syntax errors.
Writing tests before or during implementation shapes the code toward modular, extensible, testable, readable and maintainable structure.
Controlling complexity is the essence of software development; unmanaged complexity yields software that is expensive to maintain and fails unpredictably.

Keep a method's cyclomatic complexity below 10, because complexity above that taxes human short-term memory and correlates strongly with fault-proneness (one study found fault probability rising from 0.28 at complexity 11 to 0.98 at 74).
It is nearly impossible to achieve high test coverage on large functions with deeply nested logic, so low coverage is itself a signal of poor decomposition.
Define clean code operationally with metrics: close to 100% test coverage, cyclomatic complexity under 10 for every class and method, and a near-10.0 pylint score.
Use static-analysis tools (for cyclomatic complexity, duplication, and general quality) to measure code quality objectively rather than relying on visual inspection alone.
Scope coverage reporting to the module or package under test (for example nose's --cover-package or pytest's --cov=<pkg>) to isolate the signal you care about.
A successful developer designs the software to be run under automated tests from the start, seeks critical review, and expects to refactor at every step.
Decompose logic into small, single-purpose methods (each with low complexity and a docstring) so that the same behaviour is testable and readable, in contrast to one large 'mega' function.
Embed runnable examples as doctests in docstrings so documentation doubles as an executable, coverage-counted test.
Cover a module with both unit tests (each exercising one helper method in isolation) and a functional test (exercising the end-to-end behaviour), because they catch different classes of defect.
In class-based tests, initialise shared state in setUp and release it in tearDown (deleting the objects), so each test runs against a clean, independent fixture.

Generally do not allow pylint errors in source code, but recognise the tool is imperfect and occasionally warrants a deliberate, documented exception (for example errors caused by an external library).
exception: except deliberate, justified exceptions such as false positives from external libraries

statement: Configure the linter to your project's needs rather than accepting defaults blindly, since linters such as pylint are configurable and their raw output includes items you may legitimately silence.

Set up a data-science or software project for quality from the start with a standard scaffold: a Git repository, a CI config (for example .circleci/config.yml), a .gitignore, a README, a Makefile, and a tests directory.
Write a README that explains how to build the project and what it does, and include a CI build-status badge so the build state is visible.
Test Jupyter notebooks as part of the suite using the pytest nbval plugin, which executes every cell to confirm the notebook runs end to end.
condition: for projects that include Jupyter notebooks

statement: Be cautious with nbval's output-checking mode, because cells producing random images or nondeterministic output will fail on subsequent runs; prefer execution-only checking for such notebooks.
condition: when notebook cells produce nondeterministic or image output

statement: Apply the same automated-quality discipline (build systems, static analysis, repeatable processes) to data-science and notebook code as to traditional software, because the reliability need is the same.

Neither testing nor static analysis is a panacea; the real goal is not merely to solve the problem but to create something you can prove works, and overly complex, arrogant designs undermine that goal.
